chapter: Queens Terrace, Decca records and Amen
title: The Amen record under the title Hey Man
summary: Decca makes them title the record Hey Man to avoid church trouble; Mosley's Amen was months ahead of Woody Herman's.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: I notice here, when you come to play--and these are not the first records, these are only some of the records, this isn't all of them--this is different guys, here in '41 you've got Courtney Williams who is on solo.

That's when I made "Amen." I've got it right here. You know what we did? On that radio show six weeks ago, we played my record of "Amen", although it was under the name of "Hey man", but we were saying "Amen," because they were afraid-- Bob Stevens, who was our man down at Decca, called me and said now, we might have trouble with the church. It was a different era. He said you can say "Amen", but we're going to have to put on the record "Hey man". But we were saying "Amen." On this show, five weeks ago, we played my record, which I have over there, I'll get it for you in a few minutes, we played my "Amen", and Woddy Herman's "Amen".
Five months. Here's mine. October 21, 1941. It was on that same session and the same guys with Swampland and Snub Blues (phonetic spelling).
